overview: Barosaurus lentus was an exceptionally long-necked diplodocid sauropod from the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation (~155–150 Ma), closely related to Diplodocus but with proportionally longer neck vertebrae — the cervical series alone may have reached 9 metres. A mounted skeleton at the American Museum of Natural History in New York shows a rearing mother defending her young from an Allosaurus — the largest freestanding fossil mount in the world, though the rearing posture is biomechanically uncertain.

Whether Barosaurus could hold its neck vertically to browse high in the canopy, or was constrained to near-horizontal postures like Diplodocus, is debated. If it could rear vertically, its heart would have needed to pump blood 12–15 metres upward — requiring a heart of extraordinary size or an unusual cardiovascular system.

fossilSites.name: Morrison Formation — Carnegie Quarry
fossilSites.note: Classic Morrison bone quarry with Barosaurus material alongside Apatosaurus and other sauropods.

fossilSites.name: Tendaguru Formation
fossilSites.note: Late Jurassic African beds yielding Barosaurus africanus — evidence of a trans-Atlantic distribution when Africa and North America were closer.

articles.title: Discovery and distribution
articles.body: Barosaurus lentus was named by Marsh in 1890 from Morrison Formation material. An African species, B. africanus, was described from Tendaguru beds, showing that diplodocids had a wider distribution across the early Gondwana-Laurasia continents than previously appreciated. The AMNH rearing mount, installed in 1991, depicts a 14-metre-tall bipedal posture that remains controversial in terms of biomechanical feasibility.

articles.title: Cardiovascular challenge
articles.body: A vertical neck would place the head 12–15 metres above the heart — requiring blood pressure three to four times that of a modern giraffe to maintain brain perfusion. This has led to proposals of auxiliary hearts in the neck, extremely large primary hearts, or a resting brain with minimal blood flow requirements. The issue remains unresolved and is part of the broader debate about sauropod neck posture.

articles.title: Neck proportions
articles.body: Compared to Diplodocus, Barosaurus has proportionally longer individual cervical vertebrae but fewer of them — producing a similar total neck length through different vertebral architecture. The elongate individual vertebrae are heavily pneumatised (air-filled), reducing mass. This construction is analogous to engineering solutions seen in modern crane booms.

fossilRecord.formations: Morrison Formation, western USA; Tendaguru Formation, Tanzania
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Jurassic floodplains of North America and coastal environments of East Africa.
fossilRecord.evidence: Long neck vertebrae and diplodocid skeletal anatomy confirm its identity; its range documents the cosmopolitan distribution of diplodocids.

record.description: Barosaurus lentus was a long-necked diplodocid from the Morrison Formation of western North America. Several incomplete skeletons collectively document its elongated neck and relatively short tail compared with Diplodocus, but skull material is scarce and referrals need revision.
facts: The type specimen was founded on a series of tail vertebrae; better skeletons were referred later.
The famous rearing museum mount is a biomechanical reconstruction, not a preserved pose or directly observed behaviour.

review.ageReviewNote: Secure material is Kimmeridgian-Tithonian within the Morrison Formation.

evidence.material: Several complementary partial skeletons, including adult and juvenile material; skull remains are very limited.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Most of the postcranial plan is supported, but skull form, maximum size and rearing capacity remain uncertain.
uncertainties: Some referred specimens may not belong to the type species.
